Brodie’s abscess: The patient's symptoms, including a 1-year history of pain and swelling around the right ankle, bony thickening over the lateral malleolus, and a submetaphyseal lytic lesion in the distal tibia with a well-defined sclerotic margin on plain radiography, are consistent with Brodie’s abscess. The elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (68 mm at the first hour) also supports this diagnosis. In contrast to Osgood-Schlatter disease and Apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, Brodie’s abscess is characterized by its location in the bone and the presence of a lytic lesion.
Osgood-Schlatter disease: While Osgood-Schlatter disease is a possible diagnosis, it is less likely than Brodie’s abscess due to the location of the pain (below the knee vs. around the ankle) and the presence of bony thickening over the lateral malleolus. Additionally, Osgood-Schlatter disease typically resolves with rest and ice, whereas Brodie’s abscess often requires surgical intervention. Apophysitis of the tibial tubercle is also a consideration, but the age of onset and location of pain are different from the patient's presentation.
